report:
Your answer is supported: **no—hydroxychloroquine has not been shown to reduce COVID-19 deaths.**

The strongest evidence comes from large randomized trials. In the UK RECOVERY trial of hospitalized patients, 28-day mortality was **26.8% with hydroxychloroquine vs 25.0% with usual care** (rate ratio 1.09; 95% CI 0.97–1.23), i.e., no survival benefit and a point estimate toward harm: https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2022926

WHO’s multinational Solidarity trial likewise found **no mortality reduction** for hydroxychloroquine among hospitalized patients; it was dropped from the trial after interim results: https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2023184?query=recirc_top_ribbon_article_6

Regulators reached the same conclusion. On June 15, 2020, FDA revoked emergency authorization for chloroquine/hydroxychloroquine, saying the criteria were no longer met and that known/potential benefits did not outweigh known/potential risks: https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/coronavirus-covid-19-update-fda-revokes-emergency-use-authorization-chloroquine-and

Some early observational or nonrandomized reports suggested benefit, but they were vulnerable to confounding and were superseded by randomized evidence. For mortality specifically, the consistent randomized-trial signal is absence of benefit, with possible harm in some settings.
